name: Lily Parr
subtitle: Powerful left foot
story:
On Boxing Day 1920, Lily Parr was part of the Dick, Kerr Ladies side that played St Helens Ladies at Goodison Park. The ground belonged to Everton, one of the established men’s clubs. Records disagree over how many people got inside, with estimates ranging from roughly 46,000 to 53,000. Even the lower figure tells us how big a draw the match was.

Parr grew up in St Helens and became a star with a team based around a Preston factory. She could strike the ball with unusual power using her left foot. She was also part of a side with different kinds of talent. Alice Kell captained it and Florrie Redford was a prolific forward. The club’s fundraising matches helped build the audience that saw Parr play.

The FA’s December 1921 decision cut women’s teams off from affiliated grounds. Parr continued playing. That matters because a timeline that stops at the ban would miss a substantial part of her career. In 2002, the National Football Museum made her the first woman inducted into its Hall of Fame. The large gap between the Goodison match and that recognition shows how long the public record took to catch up with what spectators had seen.

name: Nettie Honeyball
subtitle: Victorian club organiser
story:
In February 1895, an illustrated journal called The Sketch published a photograph captioned with the name Nettie Honeyball. It identified her as captain of the British Ladies’ Football Club. That image gives historians evidence that she appeared in public under that name and held a leadership role. It does not settle what name she was given at birth.

Honeyball helped recruit women and organise a club at a time when playing publicly could draw ridicule. Recruitment was part of building the team. The club needed enough players to train and field sides, and it needed the public to know there was a match to watch. In March, its North and South sides played at Crouch End. Honeyball captained North, which won 7–1.

The two pieces of evidence tell different parts of the story. The magazine shows how the club and its captain were presented to the public. The match record shows what the club managed to put on. Suggestions about Honeyball’s real identity remain unconfirmed, so her work can be described with much more confidence than her private life. Her role is a reminder that a pioneering player often had to organise football before she could play it.

name: Emma Clarke
subtitle: Victorian trailblazer
story:
Emma Clarke played for the British Ladies’ Football Club during the Victorian era. The club organised its landmark North versus South fixture at Crouch End in 1895, when women were still an unusual sight in organised public football. The local historical society places Clarke on the South side. Nettie Honeyball, another figure in the collection, led North.

Clarke is remembered as a pioneering Black footballer in Britain. The surviving coverage is much better at telling us about the event than at giving us a season-by-season account of an individual player. A report can name a team and record a score without saying who trained regularly, what they did between matches or what position they usually played. That imbalance helps explain why her story is often told through a few documented appearances and later research.

In 2019 a blue plaque honouring Clarke was unveiled at Campsbourne School in north London. A girls’ football tournament was launched in her name at the same time. The plaque gives her a visible place in local history. The tournament gives young players a way to encounter that history while playing the game themselves. Both forms of recognition came more than a century after the 1895 fixture.

name: Alice Kell
subtitle: Dick, Kerr captain
story:
Alice Kell captained Dick, Kerr Ladies, the team that grew out of a Preston engineering works. During the First World War, women working in factories formed teams and found opponents through other workplaces and communities. The Preston side carried that momentum into the years after the war. Its charity matches brought in paying spectators and helped make the team known well beyond its factory.

The team had players remembered for spectacular goals, including Lily Parr and Florrie Redford. Kell’s place in its history was different. She was the captain, a role that meant leading a side whose success depended on defenders, forwards and organisers working together. In 1920 the team played against a touring French side. Fixtures like those helped turn an audience for local works football into an audience for international women’s matches.

Kell’s story also explains why team records are worth reading alongside goalscoring records. A list of scorers might tell you who finished a chance, but it would say little about who captained the side or how matches came to be staged. In the space of a few years, this factory team went from playing locally to drawing crowds and hosting opponents from overseas. Kell led the side through that change.

name: Florrie Redford
subtitle: Prolific Preston forward
story:
Florrie Redford worked for Dick, Kerr & Co. in Preston during the First World War. The factory was an entry point into organised football at a time when it could be difficult for a woman to find a team. Redford became one of the best-known scorers for Dick, Kerr Ladies, with 1921 remembered as a particularly productive year for her.

The Preston side became associated with big charity fixtures and touring opponents. Redford played alongside Lily Parr and captain Alice Kell. Their roles help explain how the team worked. A forward can finish an attack only if the side gets the ball into dangerous areas. A captain’s contribution may run through the whole match even when her name never appears among the scorers.

Redford’s peak scoring year also helps put the FA decision in context. Women’s matches were drawing attention while players such as Redford were building reputations. In December 1921 the FA told affiliated clubs to stop providing grounds for women’s matches. The restriction came in the same year as the scoring season for which Redford is particularly remembered. It changed where teams could play at a moment when their football was already attracting crowds.

name: Bella Reay
subtitle: Blyth’s goalscorer
story:
Bella Reay worked in a munitions factory during the First World War and played centre-forward for Blyth Spartans Ladies. Factory teams gave women in towns such as Blyth somewhere to play and an identity that spectators could recognise. Tournaments between those teams created local rivalries and a reason for supporters to follow results.

The Munitionettes’ Cup was one such competition in north-east England. Blyth won it in 1918, beating Bolckow Vaughan 5–0 in the final replay. Reay scored three of the five goals. The two matches tell us something a trophy photograph cannot. Blyth had to play the final again after a draw, and Reay’s hat-trick came in that second game. Her club also credits her with 133 goals in a single season. That is a season tally, a separate piece of evidence from the goals in the cup replay.

Modern supporters can see a plaque in Reay’s honour at Croft Park, the Blyth Spartans ground. The plaque ties the player to a place people still visit for football. Her story also widens the map of wartime women’s football. Preston’s Dick, Kerr Ladies are well known, and Blyth’s cup run shows how strong organised football had become elsewhere.

name: Rose Reilly
subtitle: Scotland to Italy
story:
Rose Reilly played for Scotland in the 1972 match against England at Ravenscraig. She was still a teenager when she left to make a living from football abroad. Her move took her first to Reims in France, then to Italy, where she played for clubs including AC Milan. The route matters because she had already played internationally for Scotland before her Italian club career took off.

The Scottish Football Museum credits her with eight Italian league titles and two Serie A Golden Boots. That combination reflects achievements over several seasons. The Golden Boots recognise individual scoring, while the league titles belong to the teams she played in. Reilly also represented Italy in the 1984 Mundialito, which Italy won. That invitational tournament took place years before FIFA launched its first Women’s World Cup in 1991.

Reilly’s career is a reminder that the history of women’s international football includes competitions with different organisers and different status. A player could be a professional club footballer and play in a major international tournament before the modern World Cup existed. Her place in the Scottish Football Hall of Fame reflects a career that began in Scotland and had a substantial second chapter on the continent.

name: Joan Whalley
subtitle: Preston’s teenage debutant
story:
In May 1937 Joan Whalley took a day off school to play her first match for Dick, Kerr Ladies. She was fifteen. The game at Roundhay Park in Leeds marked the coronation of George VI. Her debut came well after the FA’s 1921 restriction on affiliated grounds, which makes the venue and occasion an important part of the story. The team still found events at which it could play.

Whalley was later selected for a 1946 England XI fixture against Scotland. An XI is a team of eleven. In this case it was a representative side, distinct from the official England women’s international team that first played in 1972. Keeping those two fixtures separate lets us recognise the women who represented their countries informally before official recognition arrived.

After her playing years, Whalley appeared in a national Nike advertising campaign in 1996. By then almost sixty years had passed since her debut. That campaign put an early player in front of a new audience during the same year women’s football joined the Olympic programme. Her career connects the period when teams played wherever they could get a game with the period when the sport was receiving a much bigger public platform.

name: Patricia Gregory
subtitle: Builder of the women’s game
story:
In the late 1960s, women’s football in England had teams but little national infrastructure of its own. Patricia Gregory helped set up the Women’s Football Association in 1969. The new association gave clubs a way to work together, organise national competition and create a structure for an England side. It was formed before the FA lifted its restriction on affiliated grounds.

Gregory’s role becomes clearer if you look at England’s official international debut. In 1972 she and Elsie Cook, her counterpart on the Scottish side, worked together on practical details such as travel and finding a venue. Those jobs rarely feature in a match summary, which usually starts with the players and the score. They were part of what made it possible to field the teams in the first place.

The events came close together but each achieved something different. In 1969, clubs got a national organising body. In 1971, the grounds restriction was lifted. In 1972, England played Scotland in Greenock. Seeing Gregory across that timeline helps explain why the National Football Museum inducted an organiser into its Hall of Fame. Building the conditions for players to compete can have a lasting effect even when the organiser’s name is absent from the team sheet.

name: Carol Thomas
subtitle: England’s captain
story:
Carol Thomas made her England debut in 1974, aged nineteen, only two years after the team’s first official international. She became England’s second captain, following Sheila Parker. That made her part of the team’s first generation of leaders, while the national side was still building a regular programme of matches and tournaments.

In 1984 Thomas led England to the final of the first European competition for women’s national teams. Unlike the single-match Wembley final of 2022, the 1984 final was played over two legs against Sweden. Sweden won the first game 1–0. England won the return by the same score. Because the combined score was 1–1, Sweden and England went to penalties, and Sweden took the title.

Thomas was the first England woman to win fifty caps. A cap records an appearance for the national team, so that milestone reflects how often she played rather than how many goals she scored. Her story is easy to miss if you look only at lists of winners. England lost the 1984 final, but getting to that final and producing a player who reached fifty appearances were milestones for a national team that had played its first official fixture a little over a decade earlier.

name: Mia Hamm
subtitle: US attacking icon
story:
Mia Hamm was nineteen and the youngest player in the United States squad at the first Women’s World Cup in 1991. She played all six matches and scored twice in the group stage. Michelle Akers scored both American goals in the final against Norway. Their contributions came at different points in the same campaign, which is one reason to follow a tournament from the opening games rather than starting with the final.

Hamm was a forward who could both finish and create. A runner can make space for a teammate by pulling a defender away, or use the same movement to get on the end of a pass. Hamm’s 158 international goals show how often she finished moves. Her ability to bring others into the game helps explain why her value was wider than that number.

She won Olympic gold in 1996, then a second World Cup at home in 1999. FIFA named her its women’s world player of the year in 2001 and 2002, before she won another Olympic gold in 2004. Looking at that sequence shows two kinds of recognition. The medals depended on the US team winning tournaments. The FIFA awards recognised her performances as an individual within and beyond that team.

name: Marta
subtitle: Brazil’s creative icon
story:
Brazil’s 2007 World Cup semi-final against the United States gave Marta space to show several sides of her game in one match. She scored twice in a 4–0 win. On her second goal she used a quick piece of skill to escape pressure, then accelerated towards goal and finished. The change of speed mattered because beating the first defender only gave her a brief opening before the next challenge.

The win took Brazil to its first Women’s World Cup final. Germany beat Brazil 2–0 there, so Marta’s tournament ended with a runners-up medal. She still received the Golden Boot as leading scorer and the Golden Ball as the outstanding player. Those two awards answer different questions. One measures who scored the most. The other recognises performances across the tournament.

Marta went on to score seventeen goals across her Women’s World Cup appearances. The 2007 semi-final shows why the best way to understand that record is to look at the attacks themselves. Some goals come from arriving where the ball is going. In this example, a turn under pressure and the acceleration afterwards opened a route that had been closed moments earlier.

name: Michelle Akers
subtitle: First World Cup Golden Boot
story:
Michelle Akers ended the first Women’s World Cup with ten goals in six matches. Five came in a single quarter-final against Chinese Taipei. The final against Norway was closer. Akers scored the opening goal and later the winner in a 2–1 victory. That means half of her tournament total came in one game, but two goals in a different match decided the title.

Eight years later, the United States won the World Cup again. By 1999 Akers was contributing from a deeper midfield position. A centre-forward generally looks to threaten the goal and finish attacks. A deeper midfielder spends more time contesting the ball, supporting teammates and connecting play. Akers could affect a winning team from both areas of the pitch.

Putting the two tournaments side by side changes what you look for when judging her career. At the first edition, the goals tell a large part of the story. In 1999 a match report that counted only her goals would miss much of what she did. Her place in the history of the United States team comes from starring in different roles as the team won two titles.

name: Birgit Prinz
subtitle: Germany’s leading striker
story:
Birgit Prinz led the line as Germany won back-to-back Women’s World Cups in 2003 and 2007. At the first of those editions she scored seven goals. Germany beat Sweden 2–1 in the final, which was decided by Nia Künzer’s golden goal. Under that rule, the first goal in extra time immediately ended the game. Prinz was the competition’s leading scorer and won the Golden Ball, although it was her teammate who delivered the decisive finish.

Four years later Germany faced Brazil in Shanghai. Prinz scored the opening goal in a 2–0 win. Germany went through the whole 2007 tournament without conceding. That defensive record adds context to the way the final was won. Prinz’s goal gave her side the lead and the team’s defensive work helped make sure it never lost it.

FIFA also named Prinz its women’s world player of the year in 2003, 2004 and 2005. Those were three annual awards in succession, separate from Germany’s two World Cup wins four years apart. Together they show her effect on individual matches, her level across multiple seasons and the different ways a forward can shape a championship team.

name: Sun Wen
subtitle: China’s 1999 star
story:
Sun Wen helped China PR reach the 1999 Women’s World Cup final. The team showed what it could do in attack by beating Norway 5–0 in the semi-final. Sun scored twice in that match. In the final, China and the United States played for 120 minutes without a goal. The contrast between the two rounds shows how much the demands of a match can change in only a few days.

The final went to penalties. Sun converted her kick, but the United States won the shootout 5–4. A converted shootout kick helps a team win the tie, but it does not change the 0–0 score or count as a goal in the tournament scoring table. Sun finished with seven tournament goals and shared top-scorer honours with Brazil’s Sissi.

She also won the Golden Ball. That was a separate award for the tournament’s outstanding player and it could go to someone on either side of the final. China finished as runner-up, Sun finished level with Sissi on goals and Sun took the individual player award. Those are three different outcomes from one tournament. They help tell a fuller story than the identity of the champion alone.

name: Homare Sawa
subtitle: Japan’s world champion
story:
Japan fell behind twice to the United States in the 2011 Women’s World Cup final. Alex Morgan opened the scoring in normal time and Aya Miyama equalised. Abby Wambach then headed the United States back in front in extra time. Japan needed another goal late in the match to give itself a chance of winning.

That goal came from captain Homare Sawa. She met a corner near the front of goal and redirected it towards the net. By changing the angle of a ball that was already travelling across the goalmouth, she gave the defence little time to react. The match finished 2–2 and Japan won the shootout, securing its first title.

Sawa received both the Golden Boot and the Golden Ball. The first recognised her five tournament goals. The second recognised her performances across the competition. Her late finish stands out because of what it changed in the final, but she had already been creating chances and contributing in midfield. She went on to appear at a sixth World Cup. Reading the final as a sequence of goals gives each of Japan’s equalisers its proper place and shows why one player’s most famous moment still depended on the work of the rest of the side.

name: Abby Wambach
subtitle: Aerial goalscoring great
story:
The United States were close to going out of the 2011 World Cup in their quarter-final against Brazil. They trailed 2–1 deep into extra time. Megan Rapinoe delivered a long cross from the left and Abby Wambach met it with a header at the back post. The equaliser took the game to penalties, which the United States won.

It is easy to remember only the leap. The timing of the run and the relationship between passer and forward matter just as much. A cross has to arrive where the attacker can reach it before the defender or goalkeeper. Wambach’s movement put her at the far side of the goalmouth when Rapinoe delivered. The header changed the outcome of the tie, even though it did not end the game by itself.

Wambach scored with her head again in the final against Japan, putting the United States in front in extra time. Japan equalised and won on penalties. The two matches are a useful contrast. A decisive-looking header can create a new opportunity without settling a result. Wambach was named FIFA’s women’s world player of the year in 2012 and won the World Cup with the United States in 2015.

name: 1895 Women’s Football Match
subtitle: A Victorian landmark
story:
On 23 March 1895 the British Ladies’ Football Club put on a public match at Crouch End Athletic Ground in north London. It fielded two sides, North and South. These were sides from the club, rather than two national teams. Nettie Honeyball captained North and her team won 7–1. Emma Clarke is associated with the South side in local historical accounts.

The match attracted a large crowd and coverage in the press. That coverage is one reason we can still reconstruct the fixture. Some spectators struggled to see because much of the crowd stood at pitch level. As a record of the day, the reports show both an appetite for seeing women play and the limits of a ground that was trying to accommodate that interest.

Women had already played public matches in the 1880s. What makes Crouch End a landmark is that an organised club staged a well-documented fixture and brought the game to a bigger audience. Calling it the first time women played would erase earlier events. Calling it an ordinary match would miss why the club’s organisation and the surviving record matter. The result, the venue and the press coverage each tell us something different about how the game was taking shape.

story:
On Boxing Day 1920, Dick, Kerr Ladies played St Helens Ladies at Goodison Park in Liverpool. Goodison was Everton’s ground, so the match gave the two women’s teams access to the terraces of an established men’s club. It was a charity fixture, and Dick, Kerr Ladies won 4–0. The match took place less than a year before the FA asked its affiliated clubs to stop making grounds available for women’s matches. Goodison shows what that access had made possible. An established ground could bring players, spectators and fundraising together on a much larger scale. Teams could still play elsewhere after the restriction, but a match of this kind depended on facilities and space that were harder to secure.

name: 1921 FA Ban
subtitle: Grounds closed to women
story:
In December 1921 the Football Association told affiliated clubs in England to stop offering their grounds for women’s football. The decision was recorded in the FA’s minute book. The document tells us which institution acted and what it asked affiliated clubs to do. It also records the assumptions made about women’s suitability for football at the time.

The restriction arrived after the game had drawn sizeable crowds. The Boxing Day fixture at Goodison Park in 1920 is one example. That makes the idea that nobody wanted to see women play hard to square with the evidence. A decision about access can change who gets to play in front of a large audience even when there are players and spectators ready to take part.

The rule covered the grounds of affiliated clubs. Women continued to play at other venues, so there was football between 1921 and the reopening of affiliated grounds. What changed was access to well-equipped pitches and the audiences those grounds could hold. That reduced opportunities to stage major fixtures and raise money. The distinction matters when you read the word ban in a headline. The restriction damaged the game while leaving players and organisers looking for other ways to keep it going.

name: Ban Lifted 1971
subtitle: Grounds reopen
story:
The Women’s Football Association was founded in 1969. It brought clubs together and built a framework for competitions at a time when the FA’s 1921 restriction still affected access to established grounds. The new organisation and the change to the FA rule were related, but they solved different problems. Clubs needed places to play and they also needed a way to organise the game.

The FA’s own historical account separates two dates. In January 1970 the FA Council voted to rescind its 1921 resolution. In June 1971 the formal rule amendment went through at the FA’s annual general meeting. That amendment opened affiliated grounds to women’s matches and allowed registered referees to officiate. The two dates sometimes appear to contradict each other when they are quoted without the stages of the process.

Once the rules changed, organisers still had to build fixtures and national teams. England’s official women’s side played its first match in 1972, against Scotland. Putting the three developments side by side shows what each one made possible. The WFA helped clubs work together, the amendment removed a formal obstacle, and the international put the new national side on the pitch.

story:
On 18 November 1972 England travelled to Ravenscraig Stadium in Greenock to play Scotland. It was the first match for the official England women’s national side. Scotland led 2–0, with Mary Carr and Rose Reilly on the scoresheet. Sylvia Gore then scored England’s first official goal. The order matters because England’s first goal, its equaliser and its winner were three distinct moments, scored by three different players.

There was another difference between the teams’ circumstances. England had recently lifted its grounds restriction, while the Scottish association still restricted use of its own affiliated grounds. name: First FIFA Women’s World Cup
subtitle: China hosts the first edition
story:
In November 1991, China hosted the first women’s world championship organised by FIFA. It brought together twelve national teams. Earlier invitational tournaments had already given women experience of international competition. The new event put a tournament organised by world football’s governing body on the calendar, and it became the first edition in the FIFA Women’s World Cup record.

The United States and Norway met in the final in Guangzhou. Michelle Akers scored both US goals in a 2–1 win, finishing the competition with ten goals. She was the leading scorer, while the Golden Ball for the tournament’s outstanding player went to her teammate Carin Jennings. That distinction shows why match-winning goals and overall performance can be recognised separately.

The format also looked different from the modern World Cup. Twelve teams meant a much smaller field than the thirty-two that competed in 2023. That change is a way to trace the tournament’s growth across editions. It also puts the 1991 title into context. The United States won the first tournament in a series that would grow in size and reach, building on international football that women were already playing.

name: 1999 World Cup Final

story:
On 10 July 1999, the United States and China PR played the Women’s World Cup final in front of more than 90,000 spectators at the Rose Bowl in Pasadena. The teams could not be separated in normal time or extra time. That left a 0–0 match score and a penalty shootout to decide the champion.

Briana Scurry saved China’s third kick, taken by Liu Ying. Every US player who took a penalty scored. Brandi Chastain struck the fifth American kick and sealed a 5–4 shootout win. Her celebration became the best-known image of the final. The shot was decisive because of the earlier kicks and the save that gave the United States the chance to win with its fifth.

China’s Sun Wen won the Golden Ball as the tournament’s outstanding player. story:
On 31 July 2022 England faced Germany at Wembley in front of 87,192 spectators. Germany had already won the European championship eight times. England were chasing their first. The score was still 0–0 at half-time, so neither side had a lead to protect when the teams returned.

Ella Toone came on as a substitute. She ran onto Keira Walsh’s pass behind Germany’s defence and lifted the ball over the advancing goalkeeper. Lina Magull equalised for Germany, which meant the match ended 1–1 in normal time. England’s opening goal had created an advantage, but the equaliser meant they would have to create another one.

Chloe Kelly, also a substitute, scored from close range after a corner in extra time. England won 2–1. Both England goals came from players who started on the bench, but the chances were different. Toone used the space behind the defence and the goalkeeper’s position. Kelly reacted to a loose ball close to goal. Following the two moves helps explain how England solved different problems within the same final.

name: 2023 Women’s World Cup
subtitle: Spain’s first title
story:
Australia and New Zealand co-hosted the 2023 Women’s World Cup, the first edition with thirty-two teams. Spain reached the knockout rounds after losing 4–0 to Japan in its final group game. A group-stage defeat can be damaging without ending a campaign. The knockout rounds offered Spain a fresh match and a different problem to solve each time.

Spain beat Switzerland, then needed extra time to beat the Netherlands. In the semi-final against Sweden, Olga Carmona scored late to make it 2–1. England came through the other half of the draw, beating co-hosts Australia 3–1 in its semi-final. That set up a final in Sydney between England, the European champions, and a Spain side seeking its first senior Women’s World Cup title.

Carmona scored the only goal in the final, a first-half strike that gave Spain a 1–0 win. Her goals against Sweden and England had different match contexts. One broke a late deadlock and the other gave Spain a lead to defend for much of the final. Read alongside the loss to Japan, the title shows why one group result cannot tell you how the whole tournament will finish.
